name: Pope Leo III
causeOfDeath: Died in Rome on 12 June 816 after an illness that began late in 815, while Roman landowners were in revolt against papal rule.
title: pope who crowned Charlemagne emperor
summary: Leo III was pope from 795 to 816. Beaten and nearly mutilated by Roman opponents in 799, he fled to Charlemagne at Paderborn, cleared himself by oath in December 800, and two days later crowned Charlemagne emperor in Saint Peter's.
overview: The pope who survived an attempt to blind him, owed his throne to a Frankish king, and then made that king an emperor with the crown in his own hands.
greatestFeats: Crowned Charlemagne emperor in Saint Peter's on 25 December 800, placing the crown before the Romans acclaimed him
Refused to add the filioque to the Creed and set up the Creed without it on two silver shields in Saint Peter's
Restored Canterbury's authority over the Mercian sees, a ruling proclaimed at the Council of Clovesho in 803

birth.note: No source gives the year; German and Italian reference works place his birth about 750. The papal biography calls him a Roman, son of Atzuppius.

death.circumstance: Died in Rome after an illness that began late in 815, and was buried in Saint Peter's.

quickFacts.knownFor: Crowning Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Leo III was pope from 26 December 795 until his death on 12 June 816, a Roman churchman who rose through the papal treasury rather than the city's aristocracy. His pontificate is remembered for one scene, the coronation of Charlemagne as emperor in Saint Peter's on Christmas Day 800, but that scene closed a crisis that had nearly destroyed him.

On 25 April 799 men led by Paschal and Campulus, Lateran officials from the family of his predecessor Adrian I, dragged him from his horse during a procession and tried to put out his eyes and cut out his tongue. He escaped to Charlemagne at Paderborn, returned to Rome under Frankish escort, and on 23 December 800 swore on the Gospels that the charges of adultery and perjury against him were false. Two days later he crowned the king.

The rest of his long reign shows a pope who depended on Frankish protection without always doing what the Franks wanted. He refused Charlemagne's demand to add the filioque to the Creed, intervened in English church politics from Canterbury to Northumbria, and after Charlemagne's death executed Roman conspirators on his own authority in 815.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Leo was born in Rome, probably about 750; no source gives the year. The Liber Pontificalis, the series of papal lives kept at the Lateran, calls him a Roman and names his father Atzuppius, and the Chronicon Anianense, a chronicle compiled at the abbey of Aniane, adds that his mother was called Elizabeth. The father's name is unusual in Rome and has led historians to suggest a Greek or eastern family background, and Leo seems to have known Greek.

He did not come from the Roman nobility. His biography says he was brought up from childhood in the vestiarium, the office that kept the papal treasury, and he stayed in its service after he was ordained subdeacon and then cardinal priest of the church of Santa Susanna. By the time Adrian I died he was head of that office and one of the pope's chief administrators. Paolo Delogu notes that some of the church restorations the biography credits to Leo were probably carried out in these years, and the biography praises the energy with which he collected alms and bequests for the treasury, officially for the poor.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Almost everything written about Leo in his lifetime was written for or against him in the crisis of 799–800, and the picture depends on which side the writer took. His life in the Liber Pontificalis, composed at the Lateran, presents a devout and generous pope, lists his gifts to Roman churches pound by pound, and treats his survival in 799 as a miracle in which God restored the eyes and tongue his attackers had torn out. The Paderborn poem Karolus magnus et Leo papa, written by a poet at Charlemagne's court, mentions the mutilation five times and the healing seven, because a pope healed by God could hardly be the adulterer his enemies described.

The Frankish evidence is cooler. When Leo was elected, Charlemagne's letter of congratulation, carried by his counsellor Angilbert, told him to keep the canons, live honestly and fight simony, which reads more like a warning than a welcome. After Leo's return to Rome, Arn of Salzburg, one of the Frankish envoys, wrote to Alcuin about the pope's way of life in terms so damaging that Alcuin burned the letter. Alcuin still insisted that no one could judge the apostolic see, and it was that principle, not a verdict of innocence, that saved Leo in 800.

His own actions show a harder and more independent man than either portrait. He governed Rome as its ruler: calling the papal chair a throne rather than a seat probably began with him, and he kept founding domuscultae, estates farmed directly for the Church, against the resentment of Roman landowners. In 810 he faced down Charlemagne's theologians over the wording of the Creed, and when a second plot against him was uncovered in 815 he had the conspirators put to death under Roman law without asking the emperor.

Modern judgements divide along the same line. Some accounts treat him as a modest figure who lacked Adrian I's firmness and lived in Charlemagne's shadow, while Delogu reads his reign as a steady attempt to make the pope a sovereign in Rome beside, not beneath, the Frankish ruler. The accusations of 799 were never proved in any forum, and no surviving source allows a reader to decide whether they had any basis.

contentSections.title: Election and the Frankish alliance
paragraphs: Leo was elected on 26 December 795, the day Adrian I was buried, and consecrated the next day; the haste may have been meant to leave the Franks no opening to influence the choice. He then went further than Adrian had. With the news of his election he sent Charlemagne the keys of the confessio of Saint Peter and the banner of the city of Rome, and asked him to send envoys to receive the Romans' oath of loyalty, openly treating the Frankish king, who held the title of patrician of the Romans, as the city's protector.

Charlemagne replied with advice on how a pope should live and with a large share of the treasure his armies had just taken from the Avars. Leo spent it on Rome. His biography credits him with restoring churches across the city, rebuilding his own Santa Susanna and the church of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, and giving plate and furnishings amounting to more than 22,000 pounds of silver and 1,400 pounds of gold; in 807 alone he gave silver lamps to 119 churches, probably every church then in use. In 798, at Charlemagne's request, he also made Salzburg the archbishopric of Bavaria under Arn.

At the Lateran he built a great ceremonial hall, the triclinium, modelled on the halls of the imperial palace in Constantinople. Its apse mosaic showed Christ sending the apostles out to preach. On the arch to the left Christ gave a banner to Constantine and a symbol of office to a figure read as Saint Peter or Pope Sylvester; on the right Saint Peter gave the pallium to Leo and a banner to Charlemagne, still called king, with an inscription asking Peter for life for Pope Leo and victory for King Charles. The hall is gone, and the mosaic in the piazza of San Giovanni in Laterano is a remake of 1743 from seventeenth-century drawings.

contentSections.title: The assault of 799 and Paderborn
paragraphs: On 25 April 799, the day of the Greater Litany, Leo was riding to San Lorenzo in Lucina when armed men attacked him near the monastery of San Silvestro in Capite. They were led by Paschal, the primicerius, and Campulus, senior Lateran officials who had been Leo's colleagues there and belonged to Adrian I's family. They pulled him from his horse, tore his vestments and tried to gouge out his eyes and cut out his tongue, then dragged him into the church, beat him, locked him in the monastery and moved him by night to Sant'Erasmo on the Caelian Hill. That same night the papal official Albinus broke in with loyal men and carried him to Saint Peter's, and Winigis, Duke of Spoleto, whom Charlemagne had charged with watching Rome, took him to Spoleto.

How badly he was hurt is the most disputed fact of his life. Einhard, writing after Charlemagne's death, says flatly that the Romans tore out his eyes and cut out his tongue. The Liber Pontificalis and the Paderborn poem describe the same mutilation and add that God healed him. The Byzantine chronicler Theophanes wrote that he was blinded but kept some sight because the men blinding him took pity on him. The papal biography itself has Albinus's men find him able to see and speak on the night of the attack, which suggests the attempt failed and that the miracle answered the charge that a maimed man was unfit to be pope.

Leo decided he needed Charlemagne in person. Escorted by Frankish officers he crossed the Alps and in the summer of 799 reached Paderborn in Saxony, where the king was campaigning, and consecrated an altar in the palace chapel. Envoys from his enemies followed, accusing him of adultery and perjury and demanding that he retire to a monastery or clear himself by oath. Charlemagne decided nothing there and sent him back with Frankish bishops and counts led by Hildebald of Cologne and Arn of Salzburg. On 29 November 799 the clergy, nobles and foreign communities of Rome met him at the Milvian Bridge, and when the envoys opened their inquiry no accuser would stand by the charges. Paschal and Campulus were sent north as prisoners.

contentSections.title: The oath and the coronation of 800
paragraphs: Charlemagne came to Italy in 800 to settle the case himself. On 23 November Leo rode out to meet him at Mentana, twelve miles from Rome, the distance at which Roman ceremony received an emperor, and the next day waited for him at the top of the steps of Saint Peter's. On 1 December the king opened an assembly of Frankish and Roman clergy and nobles in the basilica. The accusers could not prove their charges, and the bishops declared that they had no right to judge the apostolic see, which by a principle found in texts falsely attributed to Pope Symmachus could be judged by no one.

That left Leo under suspicion but untried, and he cleared himself the way his accusers had proposed at Paderborn. On 23 December he climbed the ambo of Saint Peter's holding the Gospels and swore before Charlemagne and the assembly that he had no part in the crimes charged against him. The papal and Frankish accounts present the oath as his free choice; Delogu points out that an oath of purgation was a heavy loss of dignity that a pope accepted only because the alternative was a trial. The text of the oath preserved in canon-law collections has itself been questioned as a later version.

Two days later, at Christmas mass in Saint Peter's, Charlemagne knelt before the tomb of the apostle and Leo placed a crown on his head; the Romans then acclaimed him: 'To Charles, most pious Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, life and victory.' In the same ceremony Charlemagne's son Charles the Younger was anointed king. The order of the rite mattered. In Constantinople the acclamation made an emperor and the patriarch crowned him afterwards; by crowning first, Leo made the imperial title look like a papal gift. Einhard later wrote that Charlemagne would not have entered the church had he known what the pope intended, but moving the Christmas station to Saint Peter's and preparing a crown cannot have escaped him, and Delogu suggests his anger was at the order of the rite rather than at the title.

Byzantine writers saw a bargain. The Byzantine chronicler Theophanes, writing in the 810s, says that Leo crowned Charles 'repaying his debt' after the king took vengeance on his enemies, and that he anointed him with oil from head to foot, a detail the papal and Frankish accounts do not give. Within days Charlemagne, now able to act as judge in Rome, had Paschal, Campulus and their associates condemned to death for treason under Roman law; at Leo's request the sentences were commuted to exile in Francia.

contentSections.title: England: Canterbury, Lichfield and Northumbria
paragraphs: Leo inherited an English problem from Adrian I. At the Council of Chelsea in 787 Offa of Mercia had obtained an archbishopric at Lichfield, taking the Mercian sees away from Canterbury. After Offa died in 796, his successor Coenwulf wrote to Leo in 798 asking for the southern archbishopric to be moved to London, and blamed the Lichfield scheme on Offa's hostility to Archbishop Jænberht of Canterbury. Leo refused to move the see, answered that Adrian had acted because of the size of Mercia, and pressed the king to keep up the annual payment the English kings sent to Saint Peter. In the same letter he agreed that Eadberht Præn, the former priest who had seized Kent, was barred from kingship by his ordination, which freed Coenwulf to retake Kent.

Archbishop Æthelhard of Canterbury then went to Rome himself. In 802 Leo declared Adrian's grant of the pallium to Lichfield void, as obtained by misrepresentation, and restored Canterbury's authority over the southern sees. The Council of Clovesho announced the ruling in 803; Hygeberht, Lichfield's archbishop, had already given up the see and attended as an abbot. According to the Catholic Encyclopedia, the same synod, at Leo's command, forbade laymen to rule monasteries.

Northumbria drew him in as well. King Eardwulf, driven out in 806, went to Charlemagne at Nijmegen and then to Rome, and in 808 he was taken home by Leo's envoy, the English deacon Ealdwulf, together with two abbots sent by the emperor. The mission also showed the limits of trust between the two courts: on his way back from Britain Leo's envoy went straight to Rome instead of reporting to Charlemagne, and the emperor protested so sharply that something was being arranged behind his back that Leo sent the men concerned to him.

contentSections.title: The filioque dispute
paragraphs: The Creed agreed by the councils of the fourth century says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. Latin theologians had long taught that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and in Charlemagne's palace chapel at Aachen the Creed was sung with the word filioque, 'and the Son', added to it. In 808 or 809 Frankish monks on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem who sang it that way were accused of heresy by Greek monks, and wrote to Leo asking for support.

Leo agreed with the doctrine and sent the eastern churches a statement that the Spirit proceeds from both. What he would not accept was changing the Creed. Charlemagne had Theodulf of Orléans compile supporting texts, and a council of Frankish bishops at Aachen in 809 endorsed the addition and sent envoys to Rome. In meetings with them in 810 Leo held that the ancient wording must not be altered, that the Creed did not have to contain everything necessary for salvation, and that the palace chapel should quietly stop singing the addition so that the other churches of the empire would follow.

To make the point permanent he had the Creed without the filioque engraved in Greek and in Latin on two silver shields, each weighing a hundred pounds, and set up in Saint Peter's. The Franks kept the addition anyway. Rome's own mass did not include the Creed during his reign, and when Rome took it into the liturgy around the year 1000 it was sung in the Frankish form, the form the Byzantine church came to reject.

contentSections.title: The last years
paragraphs: Leo crossed the Alps again in 804. After looking into a reported relic of Christ's blood at Mantua he was met at Saint-Maurice by Charles the Younger, joined Charlemagne at Reims, spent Christmas with him at Quierzy and went on to Aachen, returning to Rome early in 805. No source gives the purpose of the journey. In 806 Charlemagne sent him the Divisio regnorum, the plan to divide the empire among his three sons, and Leo signed it; in 812 he approved the peace in which the envoys of the Byzantine emperor Michael I Rangabe had acclaimed Charlemagne as emperor.

The partnership did not extend to the succession. In 813 Charlemagne made Louis the Pious co-emperor at Aachen by telling him to take a crown from the altar, with no pope present and, as far as the sources show, none consulted. After Charlemagne died in January 814 Leo acted with new independence, sending Roman builders to repair the roof of Sant'Apollinare in Ravenna, a city whose archbishops resisted papal rule, and making its people provide the labour.

In 815 a new conspiracy of Roman nobles was betrayed to him before it could strike. Leo had the leaders seized and executed under Roman law, judging capital crimes in Rome himself where in 800 he had left the judgement to Charlemagne. Louis the Pious, alarmed, sent his nephew Bernard, King of Italy, to investigate, and Leo sent envoys to justify himself. When Leo fell ill later that year, armed landowners attacked and burned the domuscultae, estates the popes had built up out of Roman land, and prepared to march on Rome to take back what they claimed as theirs. Bernard had Winigis of Spoleto put the rising down.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Leo died in Rome on 12 June 816 after more than twenty years as pope, and was buried in Saint Peter's, where his remains were later placed in a single tomb with those of other popes named Leo. His successor, Stephen IV, was consecrated within about ten days and in 816 travelled to Reims to crown Louis the Pious, a sign that the popes meant to keep the role Leo had taken in 800.

In 1673 Clement X entered Leo's name in the Roman Martyrology, which is counted as his canonisation. The Martyrology commemorates him on 12 June as the pope who conferred the crown of the Roman Empire on Charlemagne, king of the Franks, and defended the true faith in the divinity of the Son of God.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: The coronation of 800 gave the papacy a claim it pressed for the rest of the Middle Ages: a western emperor was made in Rome, and the pope placed the crown. Charlemagne passed the title to Louis the Pious at Aachen in 813 without a pope, but later rulers still came to Rome for the imperial crown, Otto I in 962 and Frederick Barbarossa in 1155 among them.

His other legacies are smaller but concrete. The silver pennies struck in his name carry Charlemagne's name beside his own, marking the emperor as protector of Rome. In 1999 Paderborn marked twelve hundred years since his meeting with Charlemagne with the exhibition '799 – Kunst und Kultur der Karolingerzeit: Karl der Große und Papst Leo III. in Paderborn'.

Later popes used his story as a model. Between 1514 and 1517 Raphael's workshop painted the oath of 800 and the coronation of Charlemagne in the Stanza dell'Incendio del Borgo in the Vatican, and in the coronation gave Leo III the face of the reigning pope, Leo X. At Aachen, where Charlemagne was venerated, the shrine of Charlemagne shows Leo at the emperor's side, and he appears again on a gable of the shrine of the Virgin and on a reliquary of Charlemagne made about 1360–1370.

timeline.title: Born in Rome
timeline.description: Born to a father the papal biography names Atzuppius; he grows up in the papal treasury rather than a noble household.

timeline.title: Elected pope
timeline.description: Chosen the day Adrian I is buried; he sends Charlemagne the keys of Saint Peter's confessio and the banner of Rome.

timeline.title: Salzburg and the Mercian letters
timeline.description: Makes Salzburg the archbishopric of Bavaria at Charlemagne's request, and refuses Coenwulf's plan to move the southern archbishopric to London.

timeline.title: Attacked in Rome
timeline.description: Paschal and Campulus's men pull him from his horse during the Greater Litany and try to blind him and cut out his tongue.

timeline.title: At Paderborn
timeline.description: Meets Charlemagne in Saxony while envoys of his enemies accuse him of adultery and perjury.

timeline.title: Return to Rome
timeline.description: Re-enters the city under Frankish escort; the envoys' inquiry sends Paschal and Campulus north as prisoners.

timeline.title: Oath of purgation
timeline.description: Swears on the Gospels in Saint Peter's, before Charlemagne, that he is innocent of the charges.

timeline.title: Crowns Charlemagne
timeline.description: Crowns Charlemagne emperor at the Christmas mass in Saint Peter's, before the Romans acclaim him.

timeline.title: Council of Clovesho
timeline.description: The English bishops proclaim his ruling that ends the archbishopric of Lichfield and restores Canterbury's province.

timeline.title: Journey to Francia
timeline.description: Spends Christmas 804 with Charlemagne at Quierzy and visits Aachen before returning to Rome.

timeline.title: The silver shields
timeline.description: Rejects the Frankish envoys' case for the filioque and sets up the Creed without it, in Greek and Latin, at Saint Peter's.

timeline.title: Executions and revolt
timeline.description: Executes Roman conspirators on his own authority; while he lies ill, landowners burn papal estates until Winigis of Spoleto crushes them.

timeline.title: Dies in Rome
timeline.description: Dies after more than twenty years as pope and is buried in Saint Peter's; Stephen IV succeeds him.

timeline.title: Canonised
timeline.description: Clement X enters his name in the Roman Martyrology, with his feast on 12 June.
